evidence_quotes.quote: This paper reports the findings of a study to explore the household sanitation and hygiene practices associated with Clean Team toilet uptake, practices which have the potential to impact on public health.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 5 (Methods - Study design and setting)
evidence_quotes.quote: The survey covered two exposure groups; households with a Clean Team toilet and neighbouring households who had never been Clean Team customers.

How do Clean Team households compare with non- Clean Team households and with their own pre- Clean Team conditions with respect to usual place of defecation, disposal of children’s faeces and presence of soap and water at the place of defecation?

Data were collected from 199 Clean Team households and 201 non- Clean Team households in 16 poor neighbourhoods. A verbally administered, structured questionnaire was used to collect data on household characteristics and sanitation and hygiene practices.
The proportion of households where the faeces of all household members are disposed of safely.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household sanitation access and use of serviced container-based home toilets ('Clean Team'), compound latrines, and public toilets in low-income urban areas of Kumasi, Ghana.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study evaluates household defecation, child stool disposal, and handwashing-station practices associated with having a social-enterprise container-based toilet rather than examining a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor (passing references to the illegality of bucket latrines, landlord permission for indoor toilets, and public-toilet attendants' rules on emptying chamber pots are descriptive context only, not analysed exposures). Under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading, comparing adopters and non-adopters of a serviced toilet product constitutes generic project/service delivery and behavioural sanitation assessment, not a rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariff rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical mixed-methods data: a cross-sectional survey of 199 Clean Team households and 201 neighbouring non-Clean Team households, spot-check observations of household latrines and 25 public toilets, 2 focus group discussions, and 10 semi-structured interviews.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports sanitation access and usage outcomes including private versus shared facility use, usual place of defecation, safe faeces disposal across household members, functional latrine condition, and soap/water availability.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (households and individuals in 16 poor neighbourhoods of Kumasi), exposure (Clean Team serviced toilet household vs non-Clean Team neighbour and recalled pre-Clean Team status), outcomes, and cross-sectional mixed-methods design.

study_design: Cross-sectional household survey with spot-check observations, focus group discussions, and semi-structured interviews
population_and_sample: 199 Clean Team customer households (601 individuals) and 201 neighbouring non-Clean Team households (525 individuals) in 16 low-income urban neighbourhoods of Kumasi, Ghana, plus spot-checks/caretaker interviews at 25 public toilets, 2 focus group discussions, and 10 semi-structured interviews
exposure: Household uptake/possession of a 'Clean Team' container-based serviced home toilet compared with neighbouring non-Clean Team households (and recalled pre-Clean Team practices)
outcome: Usual place of defecation/latrine usage, safe disposal of adult and child faeces, private versus shared sanitation access and functional condition, and observed availability of soap and water at the latrine
rationale: Excluded under E03 (wrong exposure). While this mixed-methods cross-sectional study empirically examines household sanitation use and safe faeces disposal in low-income neighbourhoods of Kumasi, Ghana, its exposure is uptake/possession of a social-enterprise container-based serviced home toilet ('Clean Team') versus non-customer status. It evaluates sanitation product/service delivery and hygiene practices rather than a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing service access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2.
